claim: HIF1α protein was readily detectable in splenic NK cells from naïve mice immediately ex vivo.
source: We found that HIF1α protein was readily detectable in splenic NK cells from naïve mice, immediately ex vivo using anti-HIF1α (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating HIF1α expression in NK cells.

claim: There was essentially no HIF1α expression in other naïve lymphocytes directly ex vivo.
source: By contrast, there was essentially no HIF1α expression in other naïve lymphocytes directly ex vivo (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B comparing HIF1α expression across lymphocyte populations.

claim: Splenic and liver NK cells had similar HIF1α expression.
source: In addition, splenic and liver NK cells had similar HIF1α expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A comparing HIF1α expression between splenic and liver NK cells.

claim: Under hypoxic conditions as compared to normoxia, HIF1α protein expression increased in NK cells cultured in vitro.
source: Under hypoxic conditions as compared to normoxia, HIF1α protein expression increased in NK cells cultured in vitro (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C comparing HIF1α expression under normoxic and hypoxic conditions.

claim: Under normoxic conditions, IFNβ+ IL18 upregulated HIF1α expression to levels comparable to hypoxic conditions.
source: Interestingly, under normoxic conditions, IFNβ+ IL18 upregulated HIF1α expression to levels comparable to hypoxic conditions, though these cytokines did not further increase HIF1α expression under hypoxic conditions.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C comparing HIF1α expression with cytokine stimulation under normoxic and hypoxic conditions.

claim: IFNβ+ IL18 did not further increase HIF1α expression under hypoxic conditions.
source: Interestingly, under normoxic conditions, IFNβ+ IL18 upregulated HIF1α expression to levels comparable to hypoxic conditions, though these cytokines did not further increase HIF1α expression under hypoxic conditions.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C comparing HIF1α expression with cytokine stimulation under hypoxic conditions.

claim: When splenocytes were cultured in IL-15 under normoxic conditions for 16, 24, and 48 hr, highest HIF1α expression was found at 48 hr.
source: Moreover, when we cultured splenocytes in IL-15 under normoxic conditions for 16, 24, and 48 hr, we found highest expression at 48 hr (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D measuring HIF1α expression at different time points.

claim: HIF1α expression was not significantly upregulated after activation receptor stimulation.
source: In contrast, HIF1α expression was not significantly upregulated after activation receptor stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B comparing HIF1α expression after receptor stimulation.

claim: At all doses of MCMV, splenic NK cell activation was observed on day 1.5 post-infection as indicated by CD69 expression.
source: At all doses of MCMV, splenic NK cell activation was observed on day 1.5 post-infection (pi) as indicated by CD69 expression, an activation marker not expressed on naïve NK cells (Figure 1E), and concomitant with increased HIF1α expression.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E demonstrating CD69 and HIF1α expression at day 1.5 post-infection.

claim: CD69 is an activation marker not expressed on naïve NK cells.
source: At all doses of MCMV, splenic NK cell activation was observed on day 1.5 post-infection (pi) as indicated by CD69 expression, an activation marker not expressed on naïve NK cells (Figure 1E), and concomitant with increased HIF1α expression.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of CD69 as an activation marker and data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: MCMV infection at all doses was concomitant with increased HIF1α expression at day 1.5 post-infection.
source: At all doses of MCMV, splenic NK cell activation was observed on day 1.5 post-infection (pi) as indicated by CD69 expression, an activation marker not expressed on naïve NK cells (Figure 1E), and concomitant with increased HIF1α expression.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E demonstrating HIF1α expression at day 1.5 post-infection.

claim: HIF1α expression was highest at day 3 pi regardless of expression of the Ly49H receptor.
source: HIF1α expression was highest at day 3 pi regardless of expression of the Ly49H receptor that activates and induces NK cell proliferation and memory formation (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F comparing HIF1α expression in Ly49H+ and Ly49H- NK cells over time.

claim: The Ly49H receptor activates and induces NK cell proliferation and memory formation.
source: HIF1α expression was highest at day 3 pi regardless of expression of the Ly49H receptor that activates and induces NK cell proliferation and memory formation (Figure 1F).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about Ly49H receptor function.

claim: CD69 expression was not associated with differences in HIF1α expression in NK cells day 3 post MCMV infection.
source: CD69 expression was not associated with differences in HIF1α expression in NK cells day 3 post MCMV infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C comparing HIF1α expression in CD69+ and CD69- NK cells.

claim: The frequencies and numbers of NK cells in 1αKO mice were comparable to FL controls.
source: The frequencies and numbers of NK cells in 1αKO mice were comparable to FL controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and there was normal NK cell development, as indicated by CD27 and CD11b expression profiles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A quantifying NK cell numbers and frequencies.

claim: There was normal NK cell development in 1αKO mice, as indicated by CD27 and CD11b expression profiles.
source: The frequencies and numbers of NK cells in 1αKO mice were comparable to FL controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and there was normal NK cell development, as indicated by CD27 and CD11b expression profiles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B showing CD27 and CD11b expression.

claim: Expression of functional markers and receptors DNAM-1, KLRG1, and NKG2A was normal in 1αKO mice.
source: Expression of other functional markers and receptors, such as DNAM-1, KLRG1, NKG2A (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), and the Ly49 repertoire, was also normal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C comparing expression of these markers.

claim: The Ly49 repertoire was normal in 1αKO mice.
source: Expression of other functional markers and receptors, such as DNAM-1, KLRG1, NKG2A (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), and the Ly49 repertoire, was also normal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D showing Ly49 receptor expression.

claim: HIF1α is dispensable for normal NK cell development.
source: These data support previous findings that HIF1α is dispensable for normal NK cell development (Krzywinska et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by data from this study and cited previous work by Krzywinska et al., 2017.

claim: 1αKO mice showed increased weight loss as compared to control FL mice during MCMV infection.
source: During MCMV infection, however, we found that 1αKO mice showed increased weight loss as compared to control FL mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by weight loss measurements shown in Figure 2A over 7 days post-infection.

claim: Increased morbidity in 1αKO mice was coupled with an impaired ability to control splenic viral load at day 5 pi.
source: This increased morbidity was coupled with an impaired ability to control splenic viral load at day 5 pi (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by viral load measurements shown in Figure 2B at day 5 post-infection.

claim: The number of NK cells in 1αKO mice declined at day 1.5 pi and was significantly reduced at day 3 pi.
source: The number of NK cells in 1αKO mice declined at day 1.5 pi and was significantly reduced at day 3 pi (Figure 2C), consistent with the kinetics of HIF1α expression in infected WT mice (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C quantifying NK cell numbers at days 1.5 and 3 post-infection.

claim: The decline in NK cell numbers in 1αKO mice is consistent with the kinetics of HIF1α expression in infected WT mice.
source: The number of NK cells in 1αKO mice declined at day 1.5 pi and was significantly reduced at day 3 pi (Figure 2C), consistent with the kinetics of HIF1α expression in infected WT mice (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Based on comparison of data from Figure 2C with Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: FL control mice showed the characteristic expansion and contraction of Ly49H+ NK cells over 1 month of infection.
source: While FL control mice showed the characteristic expansion and contraction of Ly49H+ NK cells over 1 month of infection as previously reported (Sun et al., 2009), the 1αKO mice displayed reduced Ly49H+ NK cell expansion (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D and cited previous work by Sun et al., 2009.

claim: 1αKO mice displayed reduced Ly49H+ NK cell expansion during MCMV infection.
source: While FL control mice showed the characteristic expansion and contraction of Ly49H+ NK cells over 1 month of infection as previously reported (Sun et al., 2009), the 1αKO mice displayed reduced Ly49H+ NK cell expansion (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D comparing Ly49H+ NK cell numbers over time.

claim: Ly49H- NK cells were significantly impacted by the loss of HIF1α at day 3 and day 7 pi but not at other time points.
source: In addition, Ly49H- NK cells were also significantly impacted by the loss of HIF1α at day 3 and day 7 pi but not at other time points (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E quantifying Ly49H- NK cell numbers over time.

claim: 1αKO NK cells at day 1.5 pi had significant increases in CD69 expression compared to uninfected 1αKO NK cells.
source: Surprisingly, we found that 1αKO NK cells at day 1.5 pi had significant increases in CD69 expression, and IFNγ production with decreased KLRG1 expression as compared to uninfected 1αKO NK cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A measuring CD69 expression.

claim: 1αKO NK cells at day 1.5 pi had increased IFNγ production compared to uninfected 1αKO NK cells.
source: Surprisingly, we found that 1αKO NK cells at day 1.5 pi had significant increases in CD69 expression, and IFNγ production with decreased KLRG1 expression as compared to uninfected 1αKO NK cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A measuring IFNγ production.

claim: 1αKO NK cells at day 1.5 pi had decreased KLRG1 expression compared to uninfected 1αKO NK cells.
source: Surprisingly, we found that 1αKO NK cells at day 1.5 pi had significant increases in CD69 expression, and IFNγ production with decreased KLRG1 expression as compared to uninfected 1αKO NK cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A measuring KLRG1 expression.

claim: Changes in activation markers in 1αKO NK cells were subtly more than FL NK cells at day 1.5 pi.
source: While these changes were subtly more than FL NK cells, such changes were not readily apparent at day 3 pi (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on comparison of data from Figure 3A between 1αKO and FL NK cells.

claim: Changes in activation markers in 1αKO NK cells were not readily apparent at day 3 pi.
source: While these changes were subtly more than FL NK cells, such changes were not readily apparent at day 3 pi (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No significant differences in activation and effector markers were found between Ly49H+ and Ly49H- NK cells in 1αKO mice.
source: When we compared activation and effector markers between Ly49H+ and Ly49H- NK cells, we found no significant differences (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: HIF1α is not required for general activation of NK cells during MCMV infection.
source: Thus, HIF1α is not required for general activation of NK cells during MCMV infection and may actually restrict NK activation early in infection.
evidence: Based on data showing normal or enhanced activation markers in 1αKO NK cells during MCMV infection.

claim: HIF1α may actually restrict NK activation early in infection.
source: Thus, HIF1α is not required for general activation of NK cells during MCMV infection and may actually restrict NK activation early in infection.
evidence: Based on observation of enhanced activation markers in 1αKO NK cells at day 1.5 pi.

claim: Both 1αKO and FL mice were equally efficient killers of MHCI-deficient targets in missing-self rejection assays.
source: Both cohorts of mice were equally efficient killers of MHCI-deficient targets (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by in vivo cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In vivo cytotoxic killing function is intact in HIF1αKO NK cells.
source: Thus, in vivo cytotoxic killing function is intact in HIF1αKO NK cells, suggesting that the impaired NK cell immunity to MCMV is not related to inability to kill target cells.
evidence: Based on data from missing-self rejection assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The impaired NK cell immunity to MCMV in 1αKO mice is not related to inability to kill target cells.
source: Thus, in vivo cytotoxic killing function is intact in HIF1αKO NK cells, suggesting that the impaired NK cell immunity to MCMV is not related to inability to kill target cells.
evidence: Based on normal cytotoxic function observed in Figure 3C despite impaired viral control.

claim: Ki67 expression in bulk NK cells at day 1.5 and day 3 pi was comparable between infected 1αKO and control FL mice.
source: However, we observed a modest increase in the expression of proliferation marker Ki67 in bulk NK cells at day 1.5 pi and higher expression at day 3 pi that were comparable between infected 1αKO and control FL mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A measuring Ki67 expression.

claim: BrdU incorporation at day 3 pi was comparable between 1αKO and FL mice.
source: Similar results were seen with BrdU incorporation at day 3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), confirming that HIF1α is not required during the non-specific phase of NK cell proliferation that occurs early after MCMV infection (Dokun et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and cited work by Dokun et al., 2001.

claim: HIF1α is not required during the non-specific phase of NK cell proliferation that occurs early after MCMV infection.
source: Similar results were seen with BrdU incorporation at day 3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), confirming that HIF1α is not required during the non-specific phase of NK cell proliferation that occurs early after MCMV infection (Dokun et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on comparable proliferation markers between 1αKO and FL mice and cited work by Dokun et al., 2001.

claim: Ki67 expression on Ly49H+ cells in 1αKO mice was comparable to FL controls during MCMV infection.
source: Surprisingly, Ki67 expression on Ly49H+ cells in 1αKO mice was comparable to FL controls (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B measuring Ki67 expression in Ly49H+ NK cells.

claim: The frequencies of Ly49H+ NK cells in 1αKO and FL mice were comparable at day 3 pi.
source: Furthermore, the frequencies of Ly49H+ NK cells in both groups of mice were comparable at day 3 pi (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At day 7 pi, there were no differences in frequencies or Ki67 expression in Ly49H+ NK cells between 1αKO and FL controls.
source: At the peak of Ly49H+ NK cell expansion at day 7 pi, there were again no differences in frequencies or Ki67 expression in 1αKO and FL controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claim: During MCMV infection, selective Ly49H+ NK cell proliferation is normal in NK cells lacking HIF1α.
source: Thus, during MCMV infection, selective Ly49H+ NK cell proliferation is also normal in NK cells lacking HIF1α.
evidence: Based on comparable Ki67 expression and frequencies in Ly49H+ NK cells between 1αKO and FL mice.

claim: CFSE-labeled, HIF1α-sufficient and -deficient splenic NK cells analyzed at day 4 post transfer showed no significant differences in cell division.
source: CFSE-labeled, HIF1α-sufficient and -deficient splenic NK cells analyzed at day 4 post transfer showed no significant differences in cell division (Figure 4C) but the frequency of 1αKO NK cells was reduced compared to FL NK cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The frequency of 1αKO NK cells was reduced compared to FL NK cells at day 4 post transfer into Rag-γRc mice.
source: CFSE-labeled, HIF1α-sufficient and -deficient splenic NK cells analyzed at day 4 post transfer showed no significant differences in cell division (Figure 4C) but the frequency of 1αKO NK cells was reduced compared to FL NK cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: At 2 weeks post transfer into Rag-γRc mice, reduced numbers of 1αKO NK cells were observed as compared to FL controls.
source: At 2 weeks post transfer, reduced numbers of 1αKO NK cells were observed as compared to FL controls (Figure 4E) while all other immune cells showed comparable or even increased engraftment when derived from 1αKO mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E quantifying NK cell numbers.

claim: All other immune cells showed comparable or even increased engraftment when derived from 1αKO mice in Rag-γRc transfer experiments.
source: At 2 weeks post transfer, reduced numbers of 1αKO NK cells were observed as compared to FL controls (Figure 4E) while all other immune cells showed comparable or even increased engraftment when derived from 1αKO mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: HIF1α is dispensable for homeostatic proliferation in NK cells in vivo though ultimate expansion was affected.
source: Thus, HIF1α is dispensable for homeostatic proliferation in NK cells in vivo though ultimate expansion was affected.
evidence: Based on normal cell division but reduced NK cell numbers in Rag-γRc transfer experiments.

claim: When enriched CFSE-labeled splenic 1αKO and FL NK cells were in vitro stimulated with different concentrations of IL-2, comparable cell division was found.
source: Indeed, when enriched CFSE-labeled splenic 1αKO and FL NK cells were in vitro stimulated with different concentrations of IL-2, we found comparable cell division (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: When NK cells were quantified after 6 days of IL-2 culture, 1αKO NK cell numbers were significantly reduced compared to FL NK cells.
source: Interestingly, however, when NK cells were quantified after 6 days of culture, 1αKO NK cell numbers were significantly reduced compared to FL NK cells, though these differences were less evident at lower IL-2 concentrations (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Differences in NK cell numbers between 1αKO and FL were less evident at lower IL-2 concentrations.
source: Interestingly, however, when NK cells were quantified after 6 days of culture, 1αKO NK cell numbers were significantly reduced compared to FL NK cells, though these differences were less evident at lower IL-2 concentrations (Figure 4G).
evidence: Based on cell counting data shown in Figure 4G at different IL-2 concentrations.

claim: HIF1α controls NK cell numbers after proliferation though proliferation itself is HIF1α-independent.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that HIF1α controls NK cell numbers after proliferation though proliferation itself is HIF1α-independent.
evidence: Based on normal proliferation but reduced cell numbers in multiple experimental systems.

claim: At 3 days after IL-2 stimulation, 1αKO NK cells showed significant increases in transcripts for pro-apoptotic Bim and cytochrome c compared to FL controls.
source: At 3 days after stimulation, IL-2-activated 1αKO NK cells showed significant increases in transcripts for pro-apoptotic Bim, and cytochrome c, as compared to FL controls (Figure 5A), which was before 1αKO NK cells had significantly reduced numbers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The increase in Bim and cytochrome c transcripts in 1αKO NK cells occurred before 1αKO NK cells had significantly reduced numbers.
source: At 3 days after stimulation, IL-2-activated 1αKO NK cells showed significant increases in transcripts for pro-apoptotic Bim, and cytochrome c, as compared to FL controls (Figure 5A), which was before 1αKO NK cells had significantly reduced numbers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on comparison of data from Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Bim and cytochrome c protein expression was significantly increased in IL-2-activated 1αKO NK cells at day 3.
source: Furthermore, Bim and cytochrome c protein expression was significantly increased while protein expression of pro-survival Bcl-2 showed a significant decrease (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Protein expression of pro-survival Bcl-2 showed a significant decrease in IL-2-activated 1αKO NK cells at day 3.
source: Furthermore, Bim and cytochrome c protein expression was significantly increased while protein expression of pro-survival Bcl-2 showed a significant decrease (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression of Mcl-1 was not significantly different in 1αKO NK cells compared to FL controls.
source: However, expression of a known HIF1α pro-survival gene target, Mcl-1 (Carrington et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2006; Piret et al., 2005), was not significantly different in 1αKO NK cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and 1C, and cited references.

claim: Mcl-1 is a known HIF1α pro-survival gene target.
source: However, expression of a known HIF1α pro-survival gene target, Mcl-1 (Carrington et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2006; Piret et al., 2005), was not significantly different in 1αKO NK cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Based on cited references (Carrington et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2006; Piret et al., 2005).

claim: HIF1α plays an unexpected role in survival gene expression rather than proliferation in IL-2-stimulated NK cells in vitro.
source: Thus, HIF1α plays an unexpected role in survival gene expression rather than proliferation in IL-2-stimulated NK cells in vitro, suggesting that this effect might account for decreased accumulation of Ly49H+ NK cells during MCMV infection in vivo, despite normal proliferation (Figures 2D, 4A and B).
evidence: Based on data showing altered survival gene expression but normal proliferation in 1αKO NK cells.

claim: The effect of HIF1α on survival might account for decreased accumulation of Ly49H+ NK cells during MCMV infection in vivo, despite normal proliferation.
source: Thus, HIF1α plays an unexpected role in survival gene expression rather than proliferation in IL-2-stimulated NK cells in vitro, suggesting that this effect might account for decreased accumulation of Ly49H+ NK cells during MCMV infection in vivo, despite normal proliferation (Figures 2D, 4A and B).
evidence: Based on integration of in vitro survival data with in vivo observations of reduced NK cell expansion.

claim: During MCMV infection in vivo, 1αKO NK cells showed elevated Bim expression at day 1.5 and day 3 pi.
source: Indeed, during MCMV infection in vivo, 1αKO NK cells showed elevated Bim expression at day 1.5 and day 3 pi (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and Figure 5C, respectively), consistent with when HIF1α expression was highest (day 3 pi, Figure 1F) and the number of NK cells began to significantly decline (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and Figure 5C.

claim: Elevated Bim expression in 1αKO NK cells is consistent with when HIF1α expression was highest (day 3 pi) and the number of NK cells began to significantly decline.
source: Indeed, during MCMV infection in vivo, 1αKO NK cells showed elevated Bim expression at day 1.5 and day 3 pi (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and Figure 5C, respectively), consistent with when HIF1α expression was highest (day 3 pi, Figure 1F) and the number of NK cells began to significantly decline (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Based on temporal correlation between HIF1α expression, Bim upregulation, and NK cell decline.

claim: There was a trend for an increased ratio of Bim to Bcl-2 in 1αKO NK cells at the protein level during MCMV infection.
source: When we compared the ratio of Bim to Bcl-2 between Flox and 1αKO NK cells, we found a trend for an increased ratio in 1αKO NK cells at the protein level (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: At day 3 pi, 1αKO NK cells displayed increased apoptotic activity (46% increase compared to FL controls) when examined directly ex vivo.
source: At day 3 pi, 1αKO NK cells displayed increased apoptotic activity (46% increase compared to FL controls) when examined directly ex vivo with no difference in necrotic cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by Caspase 3/7 and Sytox-AAD staining data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There was no difference in necrotic cells between 1αKO and FL NK cells at day 3 pi.
source: At day 3 pi, 1αKO NK cells displayed increased apoptotic activity (46% increase compared to FL controls) when examined directly ex vivo with no difference in necrotic cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by Caspase 3/7 and Sytox-AAD staining data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: HIF1α regulates the autophagy gene BNIP3.
source: HIF1α regulates the autophagy gene BNIP3, raising the possibility that abnormal autophagy could account for our findings.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of HIF1α regulation of BNIP3.

claim: No significant differences in the autophagy markers p62 and CytoID were detected between 1αKO and FL control NK cells at day 3 pi.
source: However, no significant differences in the autophagy markers p62 and CytoID were detected between 1αKO and FL control NK cells at day 3 pi (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: HIF1α protein plays an important role in regulating survival, not proliferation, of NK cells during MCMV infection.
source: Taken together, these data show that HIF1α protein plays an important role in regulating survival, not proliferation, of NK cells during MCMV infection.
evidence: Based on data showing normal proliferation but increased apoptosis and altered survival gene expression in 1αKO NK cells.

claim: HIF1α-deficient NK cells manifest increased OXPHOS.
source: We verified that HIF1α-deficient NK cells manifest increased OXPHOS (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) that was previously reported but whose basis was not further evaluated (Ni et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and cited work by Ni et al., 2020.

claim: Despite absence of HIF1α in 1αKO NK cells at 3 days post IL-2 stimulation, glucose uptake was normal.
source: However, despite verification of absence of HIF1α in 1αKO NK cells by direct measurement of Hif1a transcripts at 3 days post IL-2 stimulation (Figure 6A), we found that glucose uptake was normal as uptake of the 2-NDBG fluorescent glucose analog showed no defect (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 6A and 2-NDBG uptake data in Figure 6B.

claim: The expression of HIF1α glycolytic target genes (Hrpt, Glut1, Pkm2, Hk2, Gpi1, Ldha, and Pdk1) was markedly reduced in 1αKO NK cells.
source: By contrast, the expression of the HIF1α glycolytic target genes, hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (Hrpt), glucose transporter type 1 (Glut1), pyruvate kinase M2 (Pkm2), hexokinase 2 (Hk2), glucose-6-phosphate isomerase 1 (Gpi1), lactate dehydrogenase A (Ldha), and phosphoinositide-dependent kinase 1 (Pdk1), was markedly reduced in 1αKO NK cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 1αKO NK cells showed impaired utilization of glucose and production of lactate when measured using liquid chromatography mass spectrometry.
source: Furthermore, we found an impaired utilization of glucose and production of lactate when we measured glucose metabolism using liquid chromatography mass spectrometry (LCMS) (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by LC/MS data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: No defects were found in glycolysis-independent metabolism (glutamine/glutamate pathway) in 1αKO NK cells.
source: However, no defects were found in glycolysis-independent metabolism, that is glutamine/glutamate pathway.
evidence: Based on LC/MS data shown in Figure 6D showing normal glutamine uptake and glutamate production.

claim: HIF1α affects metabolism of NK cells by supporting glycolysis.
source: Thus, HIF1α affects metabolism of NK cells by supporting glycolysis.
evidence: Based on reduced glycolytic gene expression and impaired glucose metabolism in 1αKO NK cells.

claim: NK cells are essential for early protection against virus infection.
source: Natural killer (NK) cells are essential for early protection against virus infection and must metabolically adapt to the energy demands of activation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of NK cell function in antiviral immunity.

claim: NK cells must metabolically adapt to the energy demands of activation.
source: Natural killer (NK) cells are essential for early protection against virus infection and must metabolically adapt to the energy demands of activation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cellular metabolism during activation.

claim: Upregulation of HIF1α is a feature of mouse NK cells during MCMV infection in vivo.
source: Here, we found upregulation of the metabolic adaptor hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF1α) is a feature of mouse NK cells during murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV) infection in vivo.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: HIF1α-deficient NK cells failed to control viral load, causing increased morbidity.
source: HIF1α-deficient NK cells failed to control viral load, causing increased morbidity.
evidence: Supported by viral load and weight loss data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: No defects were found in effector functions of HIF1αKO NK cells.
source: No defects were found in effector functions of HIF1αKO NK cells; however, their numbers were significantly reduced.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3 showing normal activation markers and cytotoxicity.

claim: The numbers of HIF1αKO NK cells were significantly reduced during MCMV infection.
source: No defects were found in effector functions of HIF1αKO NK cells; however, their numbers were significantly reduced.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2C-E showing reduced NK cell numbers.

claim: Loss of HIF1α did not affect NK cell proliferation during in vivo infection and in vitro cytokine stimulation.
source: Loss of HIF1α did not affect NK cell proliferation during in vivo infection and in vitro cytokine stimulation.
evidence: Supported by Ki67 and BrdU data shown in Figure 4.

claim: HIF1α-deficient NK cells showed increased expression of the pro-apoptotic protein Bim during cytokine stimulation in vitro.
source: Instead, we found that HIF1α-deficient NK cells showed increased expression of the pro-apoptotic protein Bim and glucose metabolism was impaired during cytokine stimulation in vitro.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Glucose metabolism was impaired in HIF1α-deficient NK cells during cytokine stimulation in vitro.
source: Instead, we found that HIF1α-deficient NK cells showed increased expression of the pro-apoptotic protein Bim and glucose metabolism was impaired during cytokine stimulation in vitro.
evidence: Supported by LC/MS data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: During MCMV infection HIF1α-deficient NK cells upregulated Bim and had increased caspase activity.
source: Similarly, during MCMV infection HIF1α-deficient NK cells upregulated Bim and had increased caspase activity.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: NK cells require HIF1α-dependent metabolic functions to repress Bim expression and sustain cell numbers for an optimal virus response.
source: Thus, NK cells require HIF1α-dependent metabolic functions to repress Bim expression and sustain cell numbers for an optimal virus response.
evidence: Based on integration of data showing impaired glucose metabolism, increased Bim expression, increased apoptosis, and reduced NK cell numbers in HIF1α-deficient NK cells.

claim: During infection with a cytolytic virus such as MCMV, infected cells become sources of viral replication and succumb to viral cytopathology.
source: During infection with a cytolytic virus, such as murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV), infected cells become sources of viral replication and succumb to viral cytopathology.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cytolytic virus infection.

claim: NK cells play an integral role in initiating and fine-tuning immune responses to provide protection against MCMV.
source: Natural killer (NK) cells play an integral role in initiating and fine-tuning immune responses to provide protection against MCMV.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of NK cell function in MCMV infection.

claim: NK cells carry out their role through secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines and direct killing of target cells.
source: NK cells carry out this role through two overlapping functional properties: (1) secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines and (2) direct killing of target cells.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of NK cell effector functions.

claim: MCMV elicits non-specific NK cell activation through a strong host cytokine response.
source: MCMV elicits non-specific NK cell activation through a strong host cytokine response but can also trigger specific NK cell activation in C57BL/6 mice.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of MCMV-induced NK cell responses.

claim: MCMV can trigger specific NK cell activation in C57BL/6 mice.
source: MCMV elicits non-specific NK cell activation through a strong host cytokine response but can also trigger specific NK cell activation in C57BL/6 mice.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Ly49H-mediated NK cell activation in C57BL/6 mice.

claim: The Ly49H activation receptor recognizes the viral encoded protein m157 on infected cells, triggering cytotoxicity and cytokine production.
source: In particular, the Ly49H activation receptor recognizes the viral encoded protein m157 on infected cells, triggering cytotoxicity and cytokine production that can modulate subsequent immune responses (Arase et al., 2002; Biron and Tarrio, 2015; Mitrović et al., 2012; Pyzik and Vidal, 2009; Smith et al., 2002).
evidence: Based on cited references (Arase et al., 2002; Biron and Tarrio, 2015; Mitrović et al., 2012; Pyzik and Vidal, 2009; Smith et al., 2002).

claim: Non-specific and specific NK cell responses are integrated to provide optimal NK cell responses and protection.
source: These non-specific and specific NK cell responses are integrated to provide optimal NK cell responses and protection (Dokun et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on cited reference (Dokun et al., 2001).

claim: Ly49H+ NK cells acquire properties characteristic of adaptive immunity of expansion, contraction, and generation of memory-like responses.
source: Ly49H+ NK cells subsequently acquire properties characteristic of adaptive immunity of expansion, contraction, and generation of memory-like responses (Sun et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited reference (Sun et al., 2009).

claim: During inflammation, rapid energy consumption by cells results in hypoxia, even in the presence of environmental normoxia.
source: During inflammation, rapid energy consumption by cells for activation, biosynthesis, and the generation of reactive oxygen species results in hypoxia, a reduction in oxygen levels, even in the presence of environmental normoxia.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cellular metabolism during inflammation.

claim: HIF1α is an evolutionarily conserved transcription factor whose protein expression is determined in an oxygen-dependent manner.
source: Hypoxia-inducible factor 1-α (HIF1α) is an evolutionarily conserved transcription factor whose protein expression is determined in an oxygen-dependent manner (Graham and Presnell, 2017; Kaelin, 2018; Schofield and Ratcliffe, 2004; Semenza, 2014).
evidence: Based on cited references (Graham and Presnell, 2017; Kaelin, 2018; Schofield and Ratcliffe, 2004; Semenza, 2014).

claim: When oxygen is readily available, hydroxylation of target residues on HIF1α results in ubiquitination and proteasome degradation.
source: Briefly, when oxygen is readily available, hydroxylation of target residues on HIF1α results in ubiquitination and proteasome degradation while, during hypoxia this modification does not occur, allowing for protein accumulation and translocation into the nucleus.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of HIF1α regulation.

claim: During hypoxia, hydroxylation of HIF1α does not occur, allowing for protein accumulation and translocation into the nucleus.
source: Briefly, when oxygen is readily available, hydroxylation of target residues on HIF1α results in ubiquitination and proteasome degradation while, during hypoxia this modification does not occur, allowing for protein accumulation and translocation into the nucleus.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of HIF1α regulation.

claim: Under hypoxic conditions, HIF1α targets genes that contain hypoxia-response elements (HREs) to initiate transcriptional changes for adaptation.
source: Under hypoxic conditions, HIF1α targets genes that contain hypoxia-response elements (HREs) to initiate transcriptional changes for adaption, supporting multiple cellular processes such as cell proliferation, survival, and glucose metabolism (Dengler et al., 2014; Schödel et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on cited references (Dengler et al., 2014; Schödel et al., 2011).

claim: HIF1α expression is directly associated with degree of oxygen levels and is necessary for adaptation to hypoxia during inflammation.
source: Thus, HIF1α expression is directly associated with degree of oxygen levels and is necessary for adaption to hypoxia during inflammation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of HIF1α function.

claim: Hypoxia is a fundamental characteristic of tumor environments and drives HIF1α protein expression in situ.
source: Hypoxia is a fundamental characteristic of tumor environments and drives HIF1α protein expression in situ.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of tumor microenvironment.

claim: NK cells demonstrate impaired effector functions in hypoxia in vitro that mirror tumor-infiltrating NK cells.
source: HIF1α has been considered a potential mediator of suppressive effects in NK cells, which demonstrate impaired effector functions in hypoxia in vitro that mirror tumor-infiltrating NK cells (Baginska et al., 2013; Balsamo et al., 2013; Chambers and Matosevic, 2019).
evidence: Based on cited references (Baginska et al., 2013; Balsamo et al., 2013; Chambers and Matosevic, 2019).

claim: Deletion of HIF1α in NK cells resulted in an improved ability to reduce tumor burden in two independent studies.
source: Indeed, deletion of HIF1α in NK cells resulted in an improved ability to reduce tumor burden in two independent studies, which was attributed to a dysfunctional VEGF axis or increased effector functions through IL-18 signaling (Krzywinska et al., 2017; Ni et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on cited references (Krzywinska et al., 2017; Ni et al., 2020).

claim: HIF1α supports metabolic adaptation to the tumor environment by upregulating key glycolysis genes to support cell proliferation and survival.
source: HIF1α also supports metabolic adaptation to the tumor environment by upregulating key glycolysis genes to support cell proliferation and survival.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of HIF1α function in metabolism.

claim: Ni et al. showed that HIF1αKO NK cells had higher oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) after cytokine activation.
source: Interestingly, Ni et al. showed that HIF1αKO NK cells had higher oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) after cytokine activation, presumably to compensate for poor glucose metabolism in the absence of HIF1α upregulated genes.
evidence: Based on cited work by Ni et al.

claim: Measurements of glucose metabolism in Ni et al. study showed no differences compared to control mice.
source: However, measurements of glucose metabolism showed no differences compared to control mice.
evidence: Based on cited work by Ni et al.

claim: Loftus et al. showed that glucose metabolism in NK cells was regulated by cMyc.
source: Using similar in vitro cytokine stimulation experiments, another study showed that glucose metabolism in NK cells was regulated by cMyc, and HIF1α was found to be dispensable and the absence of HIF1α had no effect on OXPHOS metabolism (Loftus et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on cited reference (Loftus et al., 2018).

claim: Loftus et al. found that HIF1α was dispensable for NK cell glucose metabolism and had no effect on OXPHOS metabolism.
source: Using similar in vitro cytokine stimulation experiments, another study showed that glucose metabolism in NK cells was regulated by cMyc, and HIF1α was found to be dispensable and the absence of HIF1α had no effect on OXPHOS metabolism (Loftus et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on cited reference (Loftus et al., 2018).

claim: The contribution of HIF1α to NK cell metabolism is incompletely understood, particularly during pathogen infection.
source: Regardless, as a caveat, the pro-inflammatory cytokines used are more associated with pathogen infection rather than a tumor environment. Therefore, the contribution of HIF1α to NK cell metabolism is incompletely understood, particularly during the pathogen infection.
evidence: Based on conflicting results from previous studies and lack of studies during pathogen infection.

claim: The absence of HIF1α in NK cells resulted in susceptibility to MCMV infection, but this was not due to an impaired effector response.
source: Compared to control mice, the absence of HIF1α in NK cells resulted in susceptibility to infection, but this was not due to an impaired effector response.
evidence: Based on data showing increased viral load and morbidity but normal effector functions.

claim: HIF1α supports survival rather than proliferation in NK cells through efficient glucose metabolism during MCMV infection.
source: Instead, we show a previously unknown role for HIF1α in NK cells during MCMV infection, supporting survival rather than proliferation through efficient glucose metabolism that is required for an optimal host response to virus infection.
evidence: Based on data showing normal proliferation, impaired glucose metabolism, increased apoptosis, and reduced NK cell numbers in HIF1α-deficient NK cells.
